newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH AGREE GREATER TRADING SCOPE FOR GASUNIE.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH AGREE GREATER TRADING SCOPE FOR GASUNIE.

text.p: Dutch natural gas marketer and distributor Gasunie NV may expand its trading interests after the government this week allowed it to extend its import and export contracts, the Dutch Ministry for Economic Affairs said.
Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs granted Gasunie permission to increase its export contracts by 240 billion cubic metres (bcm) and its imports by 120 bcm.
"The significance of this judgement is that we are becoming more and more a trading company. Before, we were just a gas supply company," said Gasunie press spokesman, Pieter Bakker.

Dutch monopoly supplier Gasunie currently exports about 40 bcm per of gas per year to Belgium, France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland, with contracts expiring from 2010 to 2018. Gasunie said it risked losing customers unless the government clarified its future capacity to export.
Essentially, we will now be able to export for another six years," said Bakker.
The Netherlands is the old man of the international gas industry, exporting from the early 1960s. As other nations are set to increase gas production, output from the Netherlands is set to decline.

Earlier this month, Petroloconsultants issued a report predicting the Netherlands would drop out of the list of leading producers by the year 2005. However, the government decision is an appreciation that there is still scope for Dutch gas exports.
"When we last prolonged our contracts five or six years ago, we thought it would be the last time we did so. It is impossible to say whether this will be the last time," said Bakker.
What is clear is that Gasunie's role as an importer is set to increase. It currently, imports about 3.5 bcm per year, principally from Norway.
In May, Gasunie signed a deal with Russia's Gazprom to import Russian gas from 2001 for 20 years, originally at a rate of one bcm a year, but rising to four bcm.

Norwegian imports are set to increase and, from 1998, the Netherlands expects to import British gas via the Interconnector pipeline. This month, a distributor in the south of the country said it planned to build a pipeline to the Belgian border and im port gas itself, thus breaking Gasunie's position as monopoly supplier.
